editor_spans.body: The speech adds something the press release did not have: an offer of 'DWP devolution'. My earlier note said Westminster cannot create Scottish regional bodies itself, because local government is Holyrood's business. Employment support is different. The Department for Work and Pensions is reserved, so this is the one item in the package that is London's to give away, not something Holyrood is being asked to give up. That makes it the real test of whether the offer is genuine.

There are two catches. First, Scotland already received part of this power under the Scotland Act 2016: contracted employment programmes for disabled and long-term unemployed people. Holyrood ran those nationally, not region by region. Handing over more is unlikely to produce the 'Easterhouse principle' on its own, unless the money is tied to delivery below Holyrood, which a UK Prime Minister cannot impose. Second, the same speech promises not to tolerate 'kids in their 20s just being there on benefits' and points to the Milburn review. If jobcentre support is devolved while the rules on conditions and sanctions stay in London, Scottish bodies would be giving the help while Westminster decides the penalties. That split has strained earlier devolution deals. Watch which side of that line the National Economic Council offer falls on.

His claim that Scotland is 'one of the most centralised nations in Europe' has history behind it, and he leaves it out. Scotland has 32 councils serving about 5.5 million people, so its councils are among the largest in Europe by population. Since devolution, Holyrood has also merged regional police and fire services into national bodies and for years capped what councils could raise in tax. Much of the centralisation he describes was decided in Edinburgh, not imposed by London. That is why his offer reads as a challenge to the SNP's own record, even as he says he is 'not scoring points'. It also explains why the Scottish Government's own local government reform programme is the real competitor to his plan.

Underneath the speech is an argument about who decides industrial closures. Ravenscraig in 1992 and the Lancashire pits in the 1990s both closed with no plan for what came next, decided 'hundreds of miles away'. His remedies are in two places. Procurement, like his Greater Manchester bus orders from Alexander Dennis in Falkirk, is a central lever. Regional control is a local one. In the cases he cites, Grangemouth, shipbuilding and Aberdeen's energy jobs, the outcome still rests on decisions by central government and private owners. The speech does not say what a Lanarkshire or Aberdeen regional body could do if a plant owner decided to leave.

  · The Prime Minister's own words show why London cares so much about an energy ceasefire in particular.
